# Arrays and hypergraphs

Arrays of any order, their contraction by index specification, hypergraphs, and pictures of all of them. Run a cell with **Shift + Enter**; edit anything and run it again.

m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
ArrayMultiply([m, m], "ij,jk->ik")

## One operation, many products

An index specification names the indices of each array; repeated indices are summed. The outer product of two vectors keeps both indices:
ArrayMultiply([[1, 2, 3], [10, 20]], "i,j->ij")
A trace contracts every index, leaving an array of order $0$. Without `->`, the indices that occur once survive, in sorted order.
ArrayMultiply([m], "ii->")

## Special arrays and symmetry

`IdentityArray(n, d)` is $1$ where all $n$ indices agree. At order $3$ it is drawn as a row of matrices, the first index choosing the matrix.
IdentityArray(3, 2)
A declared symmetry is checked against the entries. In a symbolic array, index tuples that the symmetry makes equivalent name one entry:
GenerateSymbolicArray(a, [3, 3], "Symmetric")

## The fish product

The ternary products of *Heaps of Fish* (arXiv:2205.05456) are contractions of three $3$-arrays. One entry of the fish product $\sum_{q,r,s} x_{ijq}\, y_{rsq}\, z_{rsk}$:

x = GenerateSymbolicArray("x", [2, 2, 2])
y = GenerateSymbolicArray("y", [2, 2, 2])
z = GenerateSymbolicArray("z", [2, 2, 2])
fish = ArrayMultiply([x, y, z], "ijp,qrp,qrk->ijk")
fish[1, 1, 1]

## Definitions and their sources

Every definition lives in the research registry, with the reference implementation and paper it comes from.
Concept("hypermatrix.array_multiply")

## Large computations

Each contraction is estimated before it runs. This one is over the browser's budget, so it is refused before any work is done; a Hyperiad server can run it.

big = OneArray(3, 120)
ArrayMultiply([big, big], "ijk,jkl->il")

## Hypergraphs

A hypergraph is a multiset of hyperedges. Each edge lists its vertices and has a symmetry type: directed (the default), unordered or cyclic. Binary edges are lines, larger edges are regions, a unary edge is a disk round its vertex.

A directed hyperedge shows its order with half-arrowheads inside the region, growing along the sequence $v_1 \to v_2 \to \dots \to v_k \to v_1$. Edges are stored in the canonical order of their symmetry, so the same hyperedge written two ways is one edge:
[Edge([3, 1, 2], "Cyclic") == Edge([1, 2, 3], "Cyclic"), Edge([1, 3, 2], "Cyclic") == Edge([1, 2, 3], "Cyclic")]
Labels are written beside what they name; `Highlight` marks edges in red, as the paclet marks the match of a rewrite rule.

g = Hypergraph([Vertex(1, "a"), Vertex(2, "b")], [Edge([1, 2, 3], "Cyclic"), Edge([3, 4], "Directed", "f"), Edge([4, 5, 5])])
HypergraphPlot(g, VertexLabels = true, Highlight = [2])

## Isomorphism and canonical forms

Two hypergraphs are isomorphic when renaming vertices carries one onto the other, each edge keeping its symmetry type. Labels count only up to renaming: `A, B, C` along a path is isomorphic to `C, B, A` by exchanging `A` and `C`.

l1 = Hypergraph([Vertex(1, "A"), Vertex(2, "B"), Vertex(3, "C")], [[1, 2], [2, 3]])
l3 = Hypergraph([Vertex(1, "C"), Vertex(2, "B"), Vertex(3, "A")], [[1, 2], [2, 3]])
FindHypergraphIsomorphism(l1, l3, Labels = true)
The canonical form renames vertices $1, \dots, n$ and replaces labels by tokens $\ell_1, \ell_2, \dots$, so isomorphic hypergraphs have equal canonical forms.

x1 = Hypergraph([Edge([1, 2, 3], "Unordered"), Edge([3, 4], "Directed", "f"), Edge([1, 4, 5], "Cyclic")])
x2 = Hypergraph([Edge([30, 20, 10], "Unordered"), Edge([30, 40], "Directed", "g"), Edge([40, 50, 10], "Cyclic")])
[IsomorphicHypergraphQ(x1, x2), CanonicalHypergraph(x1) == CanonicalHypergraph(x2)]
CanonicalHypergraph(x1)

## Rewrite rules

A rule is a pair of hypergraphs, drawn input → output on a shared layout; the vertices it creates are red. Applying it to a hypergraph gives one **event** per way its input matches: the match in red on the left, what was made in red on the right.
sub = HypergraphRule([[1, 2]], [[1, 3], [3, 2]])
sub(Hypergraph([[1, 2], [2, 3]]))

In a rule's input, a label that is a bare name is a **variable**: it binds whatever label it meets, and the output's labels are written in terms of it. This composes two arrows into one named after both:

compose = HypergraphRule([Edge([1, 2], "Directed", a), Edge([2, 3], "Directed", b)], [Edge([1, 3], "Directed", Row(["(", a, b, ")"]))])
compose(Hypergraph([Edge([1, 2], "Directed", "f"), Edge([2, 3], "Directed", "g"), Edge([3, 4], "Directed", "k")]))

## Rewriting systems and causality

A rewriting system is rules with a state to start from. Its evolution applies every rule in every way to every state of the last generation; the **evolution graph** is the tree of states it reaches, each drawn.

meet = HypergraphRewritingSystem(sub, Hypergraph([[1, 2], [2, 3]]))
meet("EvolutionGraph", 2)

The **causal graph** has one vertex per event, drawn as the event, and an edge from an event to a later one on the same path that touches some of the same elements. What counts as touching is the option `CausalDependence`: `"Elements"` (any shared vertex or edge, the default), `"Edges"` or `"Vertices"`. Two subdivisions that meet only at a vertex are related by elements but not by edges:
[meet("CausalGraph", 2)["EdgeCount"], meet("CausalGraph", 2, CausalDependence = "Edges")["EdgeCount"]]
meet("CausalGraph", 2, CausalDependence = "Edges")

## Hypergraphs as hypermatrices

An edge of arity $k$ is an index tuple of an array of order $k$, and the symmetry types correspond: Directed ↔ Rigid, Cyclic ↔ Cyclic, Unordered ↔ Symmetric. The **adjacency hypermatrix** has one array per arity and symmetry type, indexed by the vertices in order; each entry counts the edges sitting there, up to the symmetry.
adj = Hypergraph([Edge([1, 2, 3], "Unordered"), Edge([3, 4]), Edge([1, 2])])
AdjacencyHypermatrix(adj)
Renaming the vertices permutes the indices, so isomorphic hypergraphs can have different adjacency hypermatrices; after `CanonicalHypergraph` they agree.

other = Hypergraph([Edge(["z", "a", "m"], "Unordered"), Edge(["m", "q"]), Edge(["z", "a"])])
[AdjacencyHypermatrix(adj) == AdjacencyHypermatrix(other), AdjacencyHypermatrix(CanonicalHypergraph(adj)) == AdjacencyHypermatrix(CanonicalHypergraph(other))]

## Plex diagrams

A **plex diagram** (heaps-of-fish §4) is a labelled hypergraph: edges are plexes (arrays up to the order of their indices), named by their labels; vertices are indices, and a vertex marked • is summed over. The matrix product is two plexes sharing a marked index:
mm = PlexDiagram([[1, 2], [2, 3]], [2], Names = ["a", "b"])

A plex diagram is also a rewrite rule: its plexes become one plex on its free indices, labelled by the product. Rewriting a chain of three matrices in both possible ways gives two different labels, `M(M(a, b), c)` and `M(a, M(b, c))`, with the same value: associativity as confluence.

chain = PlexDiagram([[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]], [2, 3], Names = ["a", "b", "c"])
M = PlexRule(mm, "M")
PlexEvents(M, chain)

## Identities of plex products

A term written with undefined heads, such as `Mul(a, Tr(b))`, names operations in a dictionary of plex diagrams. `PlexEqualQ` decides whether two terms are the same operation: their diagrams are isomorphic by a map fixing every variable and the output order. Transposition is the plex diagram with one plex on $(j, i)$.

`PlexTerms` lists every term in which each variable occurs once; `PlexIdentities` groups terms into identities, each drawn as the diagram its terms share (output indices $i, j$ in order, contracted ones solid dark). Over two matrices with at most three operations, every identity follows from $(a^\top)^\top = a$ and $(ab)^\top = b^\top a^\top$.
PlexIdentities(PlexTerms(ops, [a, b], MaxOperations = 3), ops)

The fish semiheap, two ways. Rewriting the long fish of five plexes with the fish rule in every order gives three terms with its value (associativity as confluence); the search over all two-operation fish terms in five variables finds exactly the instances of the semiheap axiom, 120 classes of three.

fishd = PlexDiagram([["i", "j", "p"], ["q", "r", "p"], ["q", "r", "k"]], ["p", "q", "r"], Names = ["x", "y", "z"])
long = PlexDiagram([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 6], [7, 8, 9]], [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], Names = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])
PlexIdentities(PlexNormalTerms(long, PlexRule(fishd, "F")), {"F": fishd})

fishIds = PlexIdentities(PlexTerms({"F": fishd}, [a, b, c, d, e], Order = 3), {"F": fishd})
[Length(fishIds), fishIds[1]["Terms"]]
